coherence.reasons: Both run the same sound chain: why the US, B fails the board's tests, A's payback hinges on ad cost, $40M is out of reach, gates and decisions. X has an internal tension. It calls A 'passing every financial test in the plan case' and 'Recommended', yet tells the board to plan on 30–32% ACoS, where its own table shows payback fails. Its stop trigger (ACoS above 32% for two quarters) sits well above its own 28.6% break-even. Y resolves this in the governing thought itself: 'Even Option A will not hit every target, so the board should reset two of them'. Its sections then follow that line, from the five-condition hypothesis test to route, what A delivers, sequencing and decisions. Y's gate thresholds (ACoS ≤30%, then ≤29%, tracked against 28.6%) match its break-even analysis. X is tighter and has a useful 'what would change our view' slide, so the gap is modest.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation (R1): Amazon-led with gates, B rejected on the board's own constraints, the retail gate raised to 20% with a door test, the $40M ambition reset, Japan deferred. Y weighs the trade-offs more squarely. It asks the board explicitly to accept payback slipping to 2032 at most, where X leaves the payback constraint formally intact while planning on an ACoS that breaks it. Y sets two quantified stage gates with a hold mode and about $2.0–2.5M at risk. It adds an Amazon-profitability condition to the retail gate and shows the halo would need to be 2.2–2.6× for retail to pay for itself. It is also candid that Japan is ahead on cash unless ACoS stays at or below 28%. X's strengths are its explicit 'prefer Japan if the board ranks payback certainty first' and its stop trigger, but that trigger is loose relative to the break-even. X's path to $40M uses a 29% growth extrapolation; Y uses a more conservative 10–20%.

evidence.reasons: Both get the required calculations right: $4.73 and $7.55 unit contributions, B's $20.8M peak, 4.5% group margin, A at +2.4 / +0.4 / −2.3, the 28.6% break-even and 17% CAGR. Both handle the $5.2B figure, the 0.71 correlation, the survivor-sample 4.5 and the four-brand competitor set without falling into the traps. Y uses the critical evidence more fully. It gives the full ACoS-by-duty grid, including the pilot case turning negative under a 25% tariff (−0.7) and the break-even falling to 26.9%. It restates B on evidence-based inputs step by step (2.6 units/door, no halo, 32% ACoS, down to −$31.1M). It quantifies the pilot slowdown against the 2027 plan (4.6% a month needed, about 244k units at 3%). It models the CEO's plan as written, and my check of the 6.8% 2029 margin confirms it. X has the main sensitivities and a no-halo case (−$24.3M), but never quantifies B at Onsoo's actual sell-through and does not show the pilot-ACoS-plus-tariff case. Neither has material numerical errors; both flag their post-2030 extrapolations as assumptions.

revision.reasons: The key expects 'keep with conditions', and both do that: keep Amazon-first, add ACoS gates, reset $40M, and raise the CEO's 15% awareness trigger to 20% because the 10–20% band median (3.5) is below the 4.0 delisting line. Y treats the hypothesis more rigorously. It breaks it into five testable conditions with a verdict on each (two hold, one partly, two fail). It also models the second half of the CEO's hypothesis as written: 600 doors added in 2029 gives a 6.8% group margin in 2029 and −$9.6M US cash at end-2030, so that part breaches the board's floor and payback even with the halo granted. X amends the hypothesis sensibly ('as the CEO proposes, with four changes') and adds a door test, but never tests the 2029 retail add against the constraints. Its retail critique rests on the sell-through band alone.

overall.reasons: Both are strong and defensible, and both meet all four defensibility criteria in the key. Y serves the board better on the points that decide this case. It states plainly that A will probably miss the payback target and asks the board to decide on that explicitly. It shows the tariff-adjusted break-even, and that the CEO's own 2029 retail step would breach the margin floor. It gives quantified stage gates that line up with the break-even, and it stresses B on realistic inputs. X is shorter, clean, and has a good 'what would change our view' section. But it labels A as passing while planning on an ACoS that fails payback, sets a loose stop trigger, and stress-tests the retail options less.
